subtype: Approach: considers what has already been spent and decides based on what lies ahead [Thinking]
passage:
Lalit walked home along the canal path with Chetan after the evening class at the town institute. It was the accounts course, twice a week, and Lalit had done six months of it and disliked every session.

"Six months gone," said Chetan. "If you leave now, all that is wasted."

Lalit kicked a stone. "That's the wrong question. Those six months are gone whether I stay or not. The question is the next six." He counted on his fingers. "Six more months, Tuesdays and Saturdays, four hours each. Would I rather spend those on this, or on the drawing class that starts in June?"

He was quiet for a minute. "The drawing class. I keep what I learned about spreadsheets. I don't need the certificate."

qa.q: How many months of the course had Lalit already done?
qa.a: Lalit had done six months of the course.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the accounts course?
qa.a: Lalit disliked every session and was reluctant to spend more time on it.

qa.q: What could Lalit do before leaving the course?
qa.a: Lalit could talk with the institute and family, and check whether part of the course can be kept, so that the decision rests on facts about what lies ahead.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Lalit's reasoning?
qa.a: Chetan may feel surprised, having thought that leaving meant wasting the six months, and may be persuaded by the new question.

grounding: Shows a student asking whether the next six months are worth it instead of whether the first six were wasted.
